messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Sculptor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Youssef Haddad is a 75-year-old widowed Lebanese-American sculptor who was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of functional decline and growing social withdrawal. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 75, indicating severe post-traumatic stress, and has only recently agreed to seek help after his adult daughter expressed serious concern about his well-being.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Youssef was working alone in his studio when a heavy cast-iron shelving unit collapsed onto him. The unit — loaded with tools, plaster molds, and several kilograms of raw clay — struck him across the left side of his torso and pinned him to the concrete floor. He lay there for nearly two hours before his daughter, unable to reach him by phone, drove to the studio and found him. He sustained three fractured ribs, a hairline fracture to his left clavicle, and significant soft-tissue bruising across his chest and shoulder. He was hospitalized for four days. In the immediate aftermath, what stayed with him most was not the pain itself but the sensation of his own body failing him without warning — the way the breath had simply left him, the way his arms had been unable to push the unit away, the way he had lain on the floor of a space he had inhabited for thirty years feeling utterly foreign to himself.

In the weeks that followed, Youssef found himself returning again and again to the question of why this had happened to him specifically, at this point in his life, when he had already buried his wife of forty-one years and had come to regard the studio as the one place where he still had agency. He turned the question over constantly — whether it was punishment, whether it was warning, whether it was simply the arithmetic of an aging body catching up with him. He has not arrived at an answer that satisfies him, and the question has not quieted.

What has changed most visibly is his relationship to his own body. Youssef now monitors himself throughout the day with the attentiveness of someone expecting imminent failure — pausing mid-movement to assess whether a sensation in his chest is ordinary or ominous, pressing his fingers against his ribs when he wakes in the morning, interpreting ordinary muscular fatigue as evidence of something worse. He had come to believe, with a certainty that no medical reassurance has fully displaced, that the accident had permanently altered the structural integrity of his body — that what the doctors called healing was, for a man of his age, something closer to managed deterioration. The body he had relied upon for seven decades of physical work, for the lifting and carving and shaping that sculpture demands, now felt to him like borrowed equipment he no longer trusted.

This conviction has reshaped his working life profoundly. Youssef has largely stopped working with heavy materials. He will not lift bags of clay or position large armatures, and he avoids any sustained physical exertion in the studio — the kind of full-body effort that his larger pieces have always required. What had once been a daily practice of four to six hours has contracted to brief, tentative visits in which he works in small scale or simply sits among his unfinished pieces. A commissioned memorial sculpture, accepted before the accident, remains incomplete. The gallery that represents him has grown impatient, and the relationship has become strained. Youssef does not discuss this with his daughter, in part because he is ashamed, and in part because he is certain that explaining it would require him to say aloud that he believes himself permanently damaged — a man diminished in ways that cannot be reversed.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his daughter in which she told him quietly that she was frightened — not by the accident itself, but by who her father had become since. Youssef sat with that for several days before agreeing to an appointment. He arrives at the first session guarded but not hostile. What he fears most is confirmation of what he already suspects. What he hopes for, though he has not yet found the words for it, is some way of continuing to make things with his hands — some way of being in his body again without waiting for it to betray him.
